runs.text: ao vento he facil deſe apagar. S.

lines.note: Exposure to wind makes the lamp easy to extinguish, completing the example from f220. This confirms that ao ven- on the preceding page is a repeated catchword, not an extra body fragment.
Fuji means at an unsuitable time, glossed toki narazu. The Portuguese adeshoras expresses untimeliness, not simply an unspecified hour.
Fuji ni mairu means coming at an inconvenient or improper time. Mairu is the historical polite motion verb; its direction is supplied by Portuguese vir here.
Outside the proper time completes the example translation. The entire short row is Portuguese and should not contribute a Japanese reading hint.

runs.text: Fio de papel torcido com que fechão as

lines.note: Fūji is twisted paper cord used to close letters. The scan shows u with a caron rather than the OCR i; its meaning connects directly with the sealing verb below.
Letters completes the description of the objects fastened with paper cord. This single-word physical row is a continuation, not a new entry.
Fūji, fūzuru, fūjita is the sealing verb, with the dictionary's stem and inflectional endings. Closing letters is its first definition; additional marking senses follow.
Putting a sign or mark is the additional sealing sense. The scan reads ſinal with n, not OCR r; mutrar is retained as the printed historical verb rather than replaced by an assumed modern equivalent.
Fujin means inhumanity or lack of benevolence, explained as jin narazu. Initial Ii in Iinnarazu represents ji, not a sequence of two ordinary Japanese i vowels.
Fujin no tomi wa hisashikarazu shite begins a maxim that wealth without benevolence does not last. The Japanese syntax spans the row break after shi-.
Shite horobu completes the maxim: such prosperity perishes before long. Proſperidade is a single printed Portuguese noun; OCR incorrectly separated its final de as a preposition.

runs.text: virtude não durando muito ſe destrue.

lines.note: Prosperity without love and virtue soon destroys itself. The visible initial d gives destrue, not OCR cestrue; the historical spelling is retained without modernization to destrói.
A different fujin is a wife, glossed hito no tsuma. This is not the preceding moral term despite identical roman letters.
The wife of a married man completes this fujin definition. The italic S. marks written usage; it does not belong to the Japanese gloss.
Another fujin is the king's wife. The dictionary distinguishes this royal application as its own entry, and no further status or rank should be invented from the short gloss.
Fujinsha is a person lacking compassion, awaremi no nai mono. This returns to the unbenevolent sense, not the wife senses in the two preceding entries.
Without pity and virtue completes the Portuguese description of fujinsha. Both qualities qualify the person introduced by Homẽ on the previous row.
Fujitsu, written with historical final t, is falsehood: makoto ni arazu. The final consonant is meaningful historical notation and is not expanded in the source transcription.
Fujitsu here means an unspecified day, explained as hi narazu. It differs from falsehood on the previous row; the example promises a visit without fixing a date.
Fujitsu ni sanji subeshi means visiting the temple on an unspecified day. Tera is a roman Japanese noun embedded in italic Portuguese; preserve the printed word divisions in the surrounding sentence.

runs.text: nando o dia. S. ¶ Item, Logo, & ſem

lines.note: Without specifying the day completes the visit example. A further sense of fujitsu is soon or without delay, introduced by Item rather than by a new headword.
Delay completes sem detença, without delay. The apparently contrasting unspecified-day and promptness senses are both recorded by the source and should not be reconciled by rewriting it.
Fujiyū means not free or not able to act freely, glossed jiyū ni arazu. The scan reads Fujiyǔ without the OCR's extra i after F; initial Ii in Iiyǔ is consonantal ji.

runs.text: não poder fazer algũa couſa liuremente.

lines.note: Not being able to do something freely completes the definition. The scope includes practical inability, not only political or legal freedom.

runs.text: Couſa não liure, ou o não poder fa

lines.note: Fujiyū na is the adjective corresponding to the preceding entry. The image has accented u, not OCR i, and a visible gap between Couſa and não; the final fa continues fazer below.
Doing something completes the practical-inability gloss. This is a Portuguese continuation and has no separate Japanese lexical content.
Fujiyū ni is the corresponding adverbial form. Its indentation reflects a derived form, not a new sentence in the Portuguese explanation.
Fujō is uncleanness or impurity, glossed kiyokarazu. Preserve the printed caron rather than replacing it by analogy with nearby similarly pronounced entries.
Fujo means assistance, expanded with tasuke and the historical verb tasukuru. Its unaccented o distinguishes the written form from the surrounding long-vowel entries.
Hito ni mono wo fujo suru is giving material help to someone. The example is roman Japanese and the translation resumes with Fa-zer on the next physical row.

runs.text: zer bem, ou dar ajuda, & fauor a alguem.

lines.note: Doing good or giving help and favour translates fujo suru. Portuguese alguem is the beneficiary, corresponding to hito ni in the Japanese phrase.
Fujōju is failure to finish or bring something to completion. The two Portuguese verbs define non-accomplishment, preparing the calendrical expression below.

runs.text: Dia em que ſe não acaba algũa

lines.note: Fujōjunichi is a day on which an undertaking does not reach completion. The following explanation concerns an inauspicious day, not merely an accidentally unfinished task.

runs.text: couſa principiada, por algum impedimento q̃

lines.note: Something begun remains unfinished because of an impediment. The relative q̃ links that impediment with how it is interpreted on the next row.
The dictionary attributes an omen interpretation to non-Christians, using the missionaries' term gentios. This is source attribution, not an endorsement of that religious classification.
Fujō na is unclean, returning to the impurity entry rather than the intervening non-accomplishment compound. Keep its actual accent and the Portuguese doubled m.
Fujō ni is the adverbial form of unclean. Adu. is an italic grammatical label, independent of the unaccented fujo assistance entry above.
Fuju or fujumon is a written Buddhist ritual text. The source introduces its readers as Bonzos; the definition continues with its use for the dead rather than describing writing in general.
The Buddhist clergy read the text over the deceased. This short gloss points toward a dedicatory or funerary text; the more detailed Fujumon entry below helps establish the intended usage.
Fujuku is being unripe, explained as juku sezu. Initial I in Iucuxezu represents consonantal j; neither the kana hint nor the commentary should interpret it as a separate i vowel.

runs.text: Couſa que não eſtà ainda madura

lines.note: Fujuku na describes something not yet ripe. The next row first gives fruit as a literal example, then introduces a metaphorical extension.
Fruit exemplifies literal immaturity. Permet. marks a metaphorical use, not a Portuguese verb meaning permission; the source prints the abbreviation together.

runs.text: da, ou negocio que ainda està verde, & por

lines.note: A lawsuit or business matter can still be green, meaning unfinished or not ready. This is the metaphorical application of fujuku na, not a botanical continuation.
Still to be concluded completes the description of unfinished business. The isolated infinitive belongs to por concluir across the row boundary.

runs.text: Eſcritura que lem os Bonzos por os

lines.note: Fujumon receives a fuller definition as a text read by Buddhist clergy for the dead. Its relation to good works appears in the continuation; avoid identifying a specific sutra without evidence.

runs.text: defuntos de ſuas boas obras, antes de começar

lines.note: The text concerns good works and is read before beginning a sermon. The wording may concern dedication of merit; that interpretation should not replace the actual Portuguese construction.

runs.text: apregação, ou de pois de acabar.

lines.note: The reading can also occur after the sermon ends. In apregação, the ç is partly lost, with its lower trace still visible; restore the context-supported letter rather than the OCR's impossible internal gap, while retaining the printed de pois spacing.
Fujun means disorder or noncompliance, explained as shitagawazu. The Japanese negative verb and the Portuguese outside order agree; the latter continues below.
Disorder completes des-ordem. Retain the physical line break rather than treating this continuation as another definition of an independent word.
Fumai is clarity, literally not dark, kurakarazu. The definition concerns mental light or understanding rather than necessarily physical illumination.
Understanding and knowledge specify the figurative light of fumai. The italic S. marks written usage, consistent with the compact learned compound.
Fumae is a foundation or basis. Kyōmon wo introduces a Buddhist scripture as the basis in the following example; it is part of the Japanese sentence, not a Portuguese citation title.

Kyōmon wo fumae to shite means taking scripture as a foundation. The damaged letters after fum and ye are read as a and t from the enlarged crop together with the immediately preceding Fumaye headword and to shite construction; this is a qualified restoration, not an entirely clear impression.
Basing oneself on scripture completes the foundation example. The Portuguese metaphor eſtribando connects naturally with the literal foot-bracing verb defined immediately below.
Fumaye, fumayuru, fumayeta means planting or bracing one's feet. OCR omitted the s in Eſtribarſe; the visible letter and the preceding eſtribando support its restoration.
On something completes the action of placing the feet. The complement defines the support rather than a distinct kind of footwear.
Funbaru is bracing oneself with the legs. The endings ru and atta give the verb's forms, while the Portuguese explains the stance rather than only the abstract modern meaning of perseverance.

runs.text: tendidas pera fora ſobre os eſtribos.

lines.note: The legs extend outward over the stirrups. This equestrian detail is part of the dictionary's concrete definition of bracing oneself.

Fumbatacari describes spreading the legs, as in an archer's stance. The third consonant has the tall stroke of t in the scan, not the OCR c; retain this historical form instead of replacing it with modern funbaru.

runs.text: como quando hum atira com o arco.

lines.note: Shooting a bow supplies the example stance. Hum is an indefinite person here, and arco is the bow, not an architectural arch.
Fumen means not sleeping, glossed nemurazu. The worn u was split into ui by OCR; the scan and the negative-sleep compound support Fumen.
Fumetsu, written Fumet, means not perishing or being destroyed. The image lacks the OCR's extra i after F; metsezu makes the negative meaning explicit.
Fushō fumetsu is neither arising nor perishing. The dictionary paraphrases this in terms of birth and death; its final-t spelling is retained.
Neither being born nor dying completes the compound's translation. The physical break na-cer is not repaired into a single row in Level 1.
Fūmi is good flavour, yoi ajiwai. The Portuguese has ſabor with a, not OCR o, and a word boundary after ou; both nouns concern taste rather than a general aesthetic manner here.
Fūmi ga yoi means tasting good. The first accent is weak and grave-like in this occurrence; preserve the image-aligned reading rather than automatically copying the headword's caron.
Fūmi wo fukumu means containing or possessing good flavour. The adjective bom completes the preceding example before this new one begins.
Good taste completes ter bom goſto. This isolated Portuguese continuation belongs to the flavour example, not the following letter entry.
Fumi is a letter. Fumi wo asobasu uses the honorific verb for a noble person's writing, as the following Portuguese row explicitly explains.
A noble person writes a letter in the first example. Fumi wo haiken itasu, beginning at the end of this row, is the contrasting deferential expression for reading a letter.
Haiken itasu is respectfully reading or viewing the letter. The final Fu- begins fumi in another example, preserving the printed series of epistolary expressions.
Fumi wo shitatamuru means composing or preparing a letter. The historical lower-bigrade form is retained; the Portuguese goes beyond writing to arranging the physical letter.
Arranging, folding, and closing the letter completes the preparation sequence. The final Fumi- introduces a separate example about delivering it.
Fumi wo todokuru is delivering a letter to its intended recipient. The historical verb ending kuru should not be modernized to keru in the diplomatic transcription.
The person for whom the letter is going completes the delivery gloss. Vai is the Portuguese motion verb, not a Japanese fragment.
Fumi, fumu, funda is treading or stepping. The first example is abumi wo fumu, putting one's weight on the stirrups, not the letter noun from the preceding entry.
Bracing oneself in the stirrups completes the example. The next extended Japanese illustration starts narawanu, unfamiliar or unaccustomed, across the row break.

Narawanu michi no mane wo fumi, kasanaru begins a description of difficult travel. The uncommon mane is retained from the scan; Portuguese explains the footing as stones along a rocky face, so it should not be casually replaced by the familiar modern word for imitation.
Yama no yuki wo wakete continues the image of pressing through snow among successive mountains. Vaqete represents wakete, not akete; the kana hint makes that distinction useful during review.

runs.text: cima das pedras ao longo da rocha que não e-

lines.note: Walking over stones along the rock begins the Portuguese rendering of the difficult path. Its relative clause refers to the unfamiliar route and continues below.

runs.text: ra cuſtumado andar, & rompendo pella ne-

lines.note: A route one was not accustomed to walk is followed by breaking through snow. This preserves the contrast between unfamiliar footing and the accumulated mountain snow.

runs.text: ue dos montes multiplicados hũs ſobre os ou-

lines.note: Mountains multiplied one above another translates kasanaru yama. The printed word is multiplicados, with u rather than OCR n; the phrase does not call for a new Japanese reading.

Tatara wo fumu is operating bellows by treading, here glossed as smelting metal. The scan has a capital T, not OCR F; the continuation explicitly describes foot-operated bellows. The small mark after me is retained as printed rather than normalized to a hyphen solely from the word break.

runs.text: tal, ou ferro aleuantando hũa certa maneira

lines.note: Metal or iron completes the object of smelting. The text describes raising a particular kind of bellows, continued on the next row.
The bellows are worked with the feet. Karausu wo fumu introduces another foot-operated device, a rice-pounding pestle, rather than a new sense of wind or blowing.

runs.text: Pilar arroz com pilão que ſe aleuan-

lines.note: Pounding rice with a pestle translates karausu wo fumu. The relative clause describes lifting the pestle by foot, which explains why this example belongs under stepping.
Hyōshi wo fumu introduces stepping to a rhythm. The preceding foot-lifted pestle explanation ends before this dance-related example begins.

runs.text: zer mudança com os pès em bailo, &c.

lines.note: Making changes or movements with the feet in a dance completes the rhythmic-stepping example. Preserve bailo as the source's wording rather than silently substituting modern baile.

Fumiagari means stepping up or ascending. The inflectional slot visibly prints u rather than the expected ru of agaru; retain the printed form and flag the discrepancy instead of silently regularizing the paradigm.

runs.text: cõ os pès. ¶ Itẽ, Subir algũ mõte, ou ladeira

lines.note: Ascending on foot is followed by a hunting application: climbing a mountain or slope. The abbreviated nasal spellings remain as given by image-aligned OCR.

runs.text: a descubrir a caça, palaura de caçadores.

lines.note: The purpose is to locate game, and the dictionary explicitly marks this as hunters' vocabulary. Descubrir is the historical Portuguese spelling and should not be normalized.
Fumiake, fumiakuru, fumiaketa means opening a way by treading. The q before e represents k in this dictionary's spelling; this is not an unexpected g to be substituted by modern romanization.
Michi wo fumiakuru is opening a path by walking. The historical verb form and the literal Portuguese gloss agree, and Vt is italic editorial text.
By walking completes the path-opening definition. This is the final body row; the quire signature and Fu- catchword beneath it are separate furniture.
